source.title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Female Athletes

paper.citation: Hewett, T. E., Ford, K. R., & Myer, G. D. (2006). Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in female athletes: Part 2, a meta-analysis of neuromuscular interventions aimed at injury prevention. The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 34(3), 490–498. https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546505282619
paper.abstract: Do neuromuscular training interventions reduce ACL injuries in female athletes, and what common program components, implementation demands, and compliance issues characterize the available studies? Participants: Female athletes across six randomized or prospective cohort intervention studies. Sport and level: Basketball, soccer, volleyball, and team handball; adolescent through adult and high-school through professional samples. Training or return-to-play context: Primary prevention during sport participation, not post-ACL reconstruction rehabilitation. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Studies published through 2004 with an intervention and control group; abstracts were excluded. Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six intervention studies. Exposure or intervention: Varied neuromuscular programs using combinations of plyometrics, balance, strength, agility, technique, and warm-up elements. Comparator: Untrained or usual-practice control groups. Measurements and outcomes: ACL injuries and, in some studies, broader knee injuries or performance outcomes. Analysis: MEDLINE and CINAHL searches using knee injury, sports injury, intervention, and control terms; total ACL injury counts were pooled using weighted sample sizes.
paper.tldr: This early meta-analysis informs the historical evidence base for neuromuscular ACL-injury-prevention programs in female athletes and highlights implementation components and major methodological weaknesses. Across the six studies, 29 ACL injuries occurred in trained groups versus 110 in control groups; the pooled test favored intervention training (Z = 4.31, p < 0.0001). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six intervention studies. Exposure or intervention: Varied neuromuscular programs using combinations of plyometrics, balance, strength, agility, technique, and warm-up elements. Comparator: Untrained or usual-practice control groups. Measurements and outcomes: ACL injuries and, in some studies, broader knee injuries or performance outcomes. Analysis: MEDLINE and CINAHL searches using knee injury, sports injury, intervention, and control terms; total ACL injury counts were pooled using weighted sample sizes.
paper.findings: Across the six studies, 29 ACL injuries occurred in trained groups versus 110 in control groups; the pooled test favored intervention training (Z = 4.31, p < 0.0001). Four of six interventions significantly reduced overall knee-injury incidence, while three of six significantly reduced ACL-injury incidence. Compliance definitions and rates varied substantially, ranging from 28% to 100% where reported. The authors observed that the three programs incorporating higher-intensity plyometrics reduced ACL risk, whereas those without that element did not; this component comparison was observational across heterogeneous programs rather than a randomized dismantling test.
paper.limitations: Most included studies were underpowered for ACL epidemiology, four were not randomized trials, and exposure definitions were inconsistent. Injury definitions, injury verification, program documentation, and compliance reporting were incomplete in several studies. Publication bias, heterogeneous designs and treatments, and different follow-up periods could bias the pooled result; the authors noted that odds ratios may not have been the best synthesis statistic. Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): this 2006 synthesis predates later trials and modern reporting standards, so it should be interpreted as historical evidence and checked against current systematic reviews before setting policy.
paper.practicalImplications: A multi-component, progressive neuromuscular program delivered consistently is a reasonable ACL-primary-prevention strategy for female pivoting-sport athletes. Implementation quality and exposure matter: track attendance, coaching fidelity, athlete exposure, and injuries, and avoid claiming that any single component is proven sufficient from this review alone.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. A multi-component, progressive neuromuscular program delivered consistently is a reasonable ACL-primary-prevention strategy for female pivoting-sport athletes. Implementation quality and exposure matter: track attendance, coaching fidelity, athlete exposure, and injuries, and avoid claiming that any single component is proven sufficient from this review alone. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, a multi-component, progressive neuromuscular program delivered consistently is a reasonable ACL-primary-prevention strategy for female pivoting-sport athletes. Implementation quality and exposure matter: track attendance, coaching fidelity, athlete exposure, and injuries, and avoid claiming that any single component is proven sufficient from this review alone. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
